full_judgment:
4. Leave was granted to consider the of the submissions of the respondent-appellant that the interim order is in contravention of the provisions of Article 102(4) of the Constitution, that the High Court Division passed the impugned interim order without considering and being satisfied that the said order would hot be otherwise harmful to the public interest, that the impugned interim order was wrong as it is liable to cause not only grave inconvenience to the Government but also serious loss to public revenue that the writ petitioner-respondent having not made out a strong prima facie case against the assessment of duty the High Court Division was wrong in passing the impugned order. Finally, it was urged that in the interest of protection of public revenue the High Court Division ought not to have passed the interim order and that too without any provision for a guarantee to protect the ultimate interest of the Government. 

 6. Mr. Islam highlights the salient features of Article 102(4) and then submits that the entire thrust of the writ petition is that the Customs Authority should have computed and assessed the duties and taxes on the invoice value of the imported vehicles and not on the Yellow Book Value. No challenge was thrown upon the jurisdiction of the Customs Authority to assess duties and taxes. No case was made out in the writ petition as to why the invoice value should be the basis of assessment. The writ petitioner challenged supplementary duties on the ground that it will be effective from 1-7-97 whereas he submitted his Bill of Entry on 24-6-97. The High Court Division overlooked, he submits, that under section 3 of the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931 (Act No. XVI of 1931), "where a Bill to be introduced in the Parliament on behalf of Government provides for the imposition or increase of a duty of customs or excise or sales tax the Government may cause to be inserted in the Bill a declaration that it is expedient in the public interest that any provision of the Bill relating to such imposition or increase shall have immediate effect under this Act." It is Mr Islam's submission that whenever a writ petitioner submits that a tax or levy or duty' is realisable only from the date of coming into force of the Finance Act and not earlier it is his duty to produce before the Court the Finance Bill, if the Finance Act has not yet been passed or is not available in print, for the Court to be satisfied prima facie that the proposed tax or increased rate of tax will come into operation after the passage of the Finance Act. Mr Islam has placed the Finance Bill of 1977 and the Finance Act, 1977 and submits that supplementary duty was being realised from 1993. It is not a new duty. Only the rate of duty has been increased and the increased rate is realisable from the date of introduction of the Finance Bill in the Parliament, as there is a Declaration to that effect under section 3 of Act XVI of 1931. The development surcharge may not be payable before 1-7-97 but that is so small portion of the total duty involved that it will be harmful to the public interest to prevent the authority from collecting the full duties levied before release of the goods. There is a provision for refund under section 33 of the Customs Act, 1969. Further, the writ petitioner himself offered to furnish proper bank guarantee for the balance duties and taxes, but in passing the interim order the High Court Division did not protect the ultimate interest of the Government by requiring the writ petitioner to provide a bank guarantee for the balance sum assessed by the Customs Authorities The interim order, in his submission, is the product of a total non-application of mind. He further submits that is making the interim order the High Court Division granted the writ petitioner the whole relief and he has nothing more to ask for. After taking release of his imported vehicles he can now cynically withdraw the writ petition and leave the respondent appellant in a quandary as to how to realise the duties and taxes already assessed on him. 

 8. That takes the main wind out of the sail of the writ petitioner-respondent and it appears that the appellant's various arguments on non-application of mind and the impermissible granting of the whole relief in issuing the interim order have a strong validity. In so far as Mr Islam's submissions on the failure of the writ petitioner to make out a prima facie case for issuance of a Rule Nisi we shall reserve our comments because that will prejudge the issues that are pending before the High Court Division. 

 9. But that does not preclude us from considering whether the writ petitioner made out a, strong prima facie case for issuing an interim order in the terms it has been issued. Mr. Islam's submission in respect of supplementary duties is a relevant consideration while stopping the collection of public revenue. The writ petitioner, to say the least, appears to have the prima facie liability to pay supplementary duties as imposed in the Finance Act, 1996. Why should he be allowed not to pay supplementary duties at all? The disputed increase in supplementary duties is the issue, not the duty itself. The development surcharge can wait adjudication as to whether it is effective from 1-7-97 or earlier. 

 10. We now come to the more substantive portion of the arguments advanced by Mr Islam who submits that to obtain an interim order under Article 102 of the Constitution' it is not only necessary that a strong prima facie case for interference, should be made out but it is also necessary that the balance of convenience must be so clearly in favour of them asking of an interim order that there should not be the slightest indication of a likelihood of prejudice to the public interest. He has relied upon the case of Assistant Collector of Central Excise, Chandan Nagar, West Bengal vs. Dunlop India Lid AIR 1985 (SC) 330. 

 11. The fact, of the cited case are that, by a notification dated 6-4-84 the Ministry of Finance of the Government of India in exercise of powers conferred by Rule 8(1) of the Central Excise Rules; 1944, exempted tyres from a certain percentage of excise duty to the extent that the manufacturers had not availed of the exemption granted earlier under certain other notifications. Respondent Dunlop India Ltd. was a manufacturer of tyres and the Excise Department was of the view that the company was not entitled to the exemption as it had cleared the tyres earlier without paying central excise duty, but on furnishing bank guarantees under various interim orders of Courts. The company claimed the benefit of exemption to the tune of Rs. 6.05 crore and filed a writ .petition in the Calcutta High Court and sought an interim order restraining the Central Excise Authorities from the levy and collection of excise duty. A Single Judge took the view that a prima facie case had been made out in favour of the company and by an interim order allowed the benefit of exemption to the extent of Rs. 2,93,85,000.00. 'The goods were directed, to be released on furnishing a Bank guarantee of the amount. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court upon an appeal under the Letters Patent confirmed the order of the Single Judge, but made a slight modification in that the Collector of Central Excise was given the liberty to en cash 30% of the Excise appealed to the Supreme Court and by order bank guarantee. The Assistant Collector of Central dated 15-11-84 the Supreme Court vacated the orders granted by the Single Judge and the Division Bench. The Supreme Court gave two weeks time to the respondent- company to file a counter. No counter was filed, but a learned Counsel appeared for the respondent. The Supreme Court held that it had not the slightest doubt that the orders of the Single Judge and the Division Bench were wholly unsustainable and should never have been made. The Supreme Court observed the following: 

 "There was no question of any balance of convenience being in favour of the respondent company. The balance of convenience was certainly in favour of the Government of India. Government, are not run on mere bank guarantees No governmental business or for that matter no business of any kind can be run on mere bank guarantees. Liquid cash is necessary for the running of a Government, as indeed any other enterprise. We consider that where matters of public revenue are concerned it is of utmost importance to realise that interim orders ought not to be granted merely because a prima facie case has been shown. More is required. The balance of convenience must be clearly in favour of the making of an interim order and there should not be the slightest indication of a likelihood of prejudice to the public interest. 

 12. The Indian Supreme Court in coming to this decision referred to four other previous cases decided by it, namely, Siliguri Municipality vs. Amaland Das AIR 1984 (SC) 653 Titaghur paper Mills Co. Ltd. State of Orissa vs AIR 1983 (SC) 603; Union of India vs. Oswal Woollen Mills Ltd. AIR 1984 (SC) 1264 and regretted that in spite of making it clear-several times that in a proceeding under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution grant of a stay of recovery of tax shall not be given save under very exceptional circumstances and that a grant of stay should be an exception and not a rule, the Calcutta High Court has not been following those precedents. 

 13. Mr Islam points out that in spite of the scathing .criticism of the cited judgment by HM Seervai in his Constitutional Law of India, 4th Edition, pp. 1668-1677, the Supreme Court of India has persistently followed this principle and the latest such examples are contained in the cases of State of West Bengal and others vs. Calcutta Hardware Stores and others, AIR 1986 (SC) 614 and Bank of Maharashtra vs. Race Shipping and Transport Co Pvt Ltd and another, AIR 1995 (SC) 1368. 

 14. Mr Islam submits that it is not his submission that a private interest can never represent a public interest because public interest also includes private interest. It is in the public interest not to harm a private interest irretrievably. He submits that in the cited case it has been acknowledged that there are "cases which demand that interim orders should be made in the interest of justice. Where gross violations of the law and injustice are perpetrated or are about to be perpetrated it is the bounden duty of the Court to "intervene and give appropriate interim relief. In cases where denial of interim relief  nay lead to public mischief, grave irreparable private injury or shake a citizen's faith in the impartiality of public administration, a Court may well be justified in granting interim relief against public authority. But since the law presumes that public authorities function properly and bona fide with due regard to the public interest, the Court must be circumspect in granting interim orders of far reaching dimensions or orders causing administrative burdensome inconvenience or orders preventing collection of public revenue for no better reason case than that the parties have come to the Court alleging prejudice, inconvenience or harm and that a prima facie case has been shown, There can be and there are no hard and fast rules. But prudence, discretion and circumspection are called for." 

 15. Mr Islam submits that in the present case even if it is assumed that a prima facie case has been shown yet it has not been shows at all that the balance of convenience is so much in favour of making an interim order that there should not be the slightest indication of a likelihood of prejudice to the public interest. 

 17. We asked Mr KS Nabi, learned Attorney-General, to address us on this question as amicus curiae and the substance of his submission is that with the introduction of section 196C to the Customs Act, 1969 by an amendment in 1996, a self-contained Judicial appellate authority has been created for adjudication on customs matters and provision has been made for Statement of Case to the High Court Division under section 196D of the said Act at a later stage. Therefore, the High Court Division has the opportunity to interfere under the said Act, but at a later stage. He submits that the filing of the writ petition is premature under the new dispensation and the question of granting interim order does not arise. 

 18. This argument was not advanced before the High Court Division in any case so far and we do not have the benefit of a judgment of the High Court Division on these submissions of the learned Attorney-General. If and when such a contention is raised before the High Court Division and the High Court Division gives its considered view on these submissions we may consider the same in an appropriate case. 

 (2) The first condition is that the. Attorney-General will be given reasonable notice of the application and he (or an Advocate authorised by him in that behalf) will be given an opportunity of being heard. This condition has two components, viz., (a) that the Attorney-General must receive reasonable notice of the application. A "reasonable notice" means a reasonable length of time within which it is possible and feasible for the Attorney-General to obtain instructions from relevant quarters. He or his authorised Advocate is entitled to a reasonable length of adjournment, if prayed for, to obtain instructions. What is reasonable notice will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case, but if the Attorney-General alleges and proves to the satisfaction of either Division that he was not given reasonable notice of the application one of the conditions precedent for the exercise of the power is not fulfilled and the interim order renders itself liable to interference; and (b) that he or an Advocate authorised by him has been given an opportunity of being heard. If the High Court Division is of opinion that an interim order is inextricably connected with sub-clause (a) or (b) of clause (4), the High Court Division ought to refrain from passing an interim order, fix a date for appearance of the Attorney-General or his authorised Advocate giving him a notice therefor, unless in the facts of the case the High Court Division is of opinion that the Attorney-General has already received sufficient notice of the application and there are no reasons for his or his authorised Advocate's non-appearance to make submissions on the interim order. 

 (6) It is neither possible nor desirable to lay down all the principles in advance on the basis of which a Court will come to a conclusion that an interim order is likely to have the effect of prejudicing or interfering with the implementation of any development programme or work or will be otherwise harmful to the public interest. Broadly speaking, to obtain an interim order, a writ petitioner must not only make out a prima facie case, but a strong prima facie case. The balance of inconvenience in his favour shall be so strong that it will outweigh the consideration of sub-clause (a) or (b) of clause (4). 

 (7) Generally speaking, impeding the assessment or collection of public revenues is otherwise harmful to the public interest. In cases where no jurisdictional issues are involved and when the manufacturer, trader or importer usually pass on the burden of new, additional or increased indirect taxation to the consumers, there is absolutely no justification to protect their temporary private interest by an interim order, impeding the collection of public revenue. 

 (8) Interim orders ought to be given to protect private interest when private interest is face to face with extinction or irretrievable damage. It is in the public interest to protect private interest which stands in the danger of being irretrievably damaged or faces extinction. An interim order can also be passed when the order under challenge is shown to suffer from an absolute lack of jurisdiction (as distinct from a mere difference of interpretation between various relevant authorities or between a relevant authority and the writ petitioner) or clear or patent excess of jurisdiction or patent mala fide without requirement of further proof. Interim orders may also be made in furtherance of public interest when gross violation of law is apparent on the face of the application, where grave injustices are perpetrated or are about to be perpetrated, where denial of interim relief will lead to public mischief, grave irretrievable private injury or shake a citizen's faith in the impartiality of public administration. But short of these paramount considerations, interim order should not be made when it causes administrative burdensome inconvenience or deadlock or bottleneck, impedes or prevents assessment or collection of public revenue, stays the proceedings of inferior tribunals impeding its progress when speedy trial is the object of establishment of such tribunals, stops the implementation of a development work which has to be completed within a time-frame or which is primarily financed externally on pain of lapse of financial support if not completed within a certain period and so on. Salus populi est suprema /ex—Regard for the public welfare is the highest law—and in each case the High Court Division will consider whether in spite of prima facie case and balance of convenience the individual interest should be subjugated to public interest. 

 (9) Governments are not run on bank guarantees but on liquid cash, but it is a rule of law, which has been designated as a "legal axiom", that "no pecuniary burden can be imposed upon the subjects of this country (meaning England), by whatever name it may be called, whether tax, rate, or toll, except upon clear and distinct legal authority, established by those who seek to impose the burden." (Per Wilde, CJ in Gosling vs. Veley 12 QB3 28 (407), quoted in Broom's Legal Maxims, 10th Edn, p.3). This "legal axiom" is now constitutionally guaranteed under Article 83 of the Constitution, "No tax shall be levied or collected except by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament." There is a tacit admission in section 33 of the Customs Act, 1969 that the Customs Authorities may, after all, human as they are, levy excess customs-duties or charges "through inadvertence, error or misconstruction" and there is a clear provision for refund of excess realisation if the claim for refund is made within a stated period of time. But there may be cases where there is no sanction of law at all behind a customs claim. We do not think it serves public purpose to permit the Customs authorities to realise all that they claim before they release the goods. We do not see why the Customs should be paid any sum in advance before release of the goods if the claimed amount has prima facie no sanction of law. Government cannot be allowed to run on illegal collections as well. Lest what appears to be illegal on first impression, turns out to be legal after all, a Bank Guarantee is a sufficient protection to a taxing authority's questionable demand.
